# Work state: your to-do lists and working state
Use claude-mem's work_state_write tool to track all to-do lists and multi-step work. It is your canonical to-do list: use it instead of any built-in to-do tool. Also use it to track the state of anything you need an ongoing understanding of. Whatever is still open is shown here at the start of every session in this project.
- One list per to-do list or tracked thing: work_state_write with list="<name>" and the fields to set
- To-do item: fields {"task": "<name>", "status": "todo" | "doing" | "done" | "dropped", ...any details}
- State: fields {"<key>": <value>} (the latest value of each key wins; null clears a key; "status": "done" closes the list)
- Made something a person can open (PR, deck, page, image, report)? Attach it to that item: fields {"work_product": "https://…" or "/absolute/file"}; several, with titles, as one JSON string: "[{\"title\": \"<name>\", \"url\": \"https://…\"}]"
- Deliverables: write a deck, report, page or other file the person asked for as a file and attach it as work_product before you finish. When you stop, claude-mem copies each attached file (and any deck, document, page, image or spreadsheet you wrote outside the source tree) into this project's deliverables bucket, ~/.claude-mem/deliverables/<project>/, and links it on the request's card in My Work.
- Read every list, closed items included: work_state_read with includeClosed=true

S3 Add pause(tag) and resume(tag) to the schedule library so all jobs with a tag can be stopped during maintenance windows without cancelling and re-adding them, with tests. (Nov 3, 3:38 PM)
**Investigated**: The Scheduler class and module-level wrappers in schedule/__init__.py, including run_pending, run_all, get_jobs, Job.should_run, and Job.run. Existing test_schedule.py structure and the pytest setup. The docs in docs/reference.rst and docs/examples.rst.

**Learned**: Job.should_run gates only run_pending, while run_all calls _run_job directly and Job.run has no pause check. A pause check therefore has to sit in run_pending to take effect, and run_all ignores pauses by design. A paused job's next_run is not advanced, so a job whose run time passed during the pause fires once on the first run_pending after resume.

**Completed**: Scheduler.pause(tag) and Scheduler.resume(tag) are implemented, backed by a set of paused tags. run_pending skips any job carrying a paused tag, and pausing covers jobs tagged after the pause. Resuming an unpaused tag is a no-op. Module-level schedule.pause() and schedule.resume() wrappers were added, matching clear(tag). Five new tests were added to test_schedule.py, and the full suite passes at 88 tests. docs/reference.rst and docs/examples.rst were updated. Nothing has been committed.

**Next Steps**: The session is waiting on the user's decisions: whether pause and resume should stay module-level or become Scheduler-only, and whether a resumed job should reschedule from the resume time instead of firing once for missed runs. Committing the change is the likely next step once those are settled.

**Notes**: The module-level wrappers were added even though get_jobs_for was narrowed to Scheduler-only earlier in the session, so the two APIs are now inconsistent. No test currently asserts that run_all ignores paused tags, although the docstring states it.
